title: AI’s Historical Present: This Part Is Still Mine
author: James Hutson
source: nickpotkalitsky.substack.com (guest post by James Hutson), October 19, 2026
summary: James Hutson, Director of AI-Enabled Academic Transformation at Lindenwood University, looks back from 2026 at an eight-week web design course in spring 2023 where students were deliberately introduced to text and image generators. In week eight the requirement to mention AI was removed, yet 87.5 percent still incorporated AI applications into their final projects. A survey showed students more willing to allow AI during ideation (78.13 percent) than to complete final work (65.63 percent), which Hutson reads as an early distinction between assistance and substitution. A 2024 follow-up found adoption varied with disciplinary identity, with computer science students more willing to use AI for color selection than for coding. He argues the key variable is not how much of an artifact a machine touched but where the student's intellectual agency remained active. The lasting lesson is that the boundary a learner draws between assistance and authorship is itself the most important evidence.
points: When the requirement to disclose AI use was removed, most students still chose to use it, showing a shift from compliance to independent judgment.
Students separated assistance from substitution, supporting AI in ideation far more than in submitting final work.
Adoption followed disciplinary identity, with students sharing tasks outside their core expertise with AI more readily than tasks central to it.
Permission structures matter less than where a student's judgment, criticism and revision stay active.
Teachers can treat the boundary students draw between assisted and authored work as evidence of learning.
quotes: What is important is that most had moved from complying with an instructional exercise to making an independent decision about whether a tool belonged in their work.
Students seemed to understand assistance and substitution as different categories even when faculty policy had not yet developed precise language for the distinction.

In 2023, much of the conversation focused on whether AI use counted as cheating. The students were already confronting a harder problem, namely how much cognitive and creative responsibility they were willing to delegate.

Students were not simply deciding whether AI was useful; they were deciding which forms of expertise they were prepared to share with it. The question of tool adoption had quietly become a question of professional and intellectual identity.

A student can use AI extensively and still exercise substantial judgment, criticism, revision, and disciplinary knowledge; another can use much less AI and surrender the thinking an assignment was designed to elicit.
The surprising result was not that most students used AI when they were given the choice. It was that choice itself became data.
Instead, 87.5% incorporated AI applications into their final projects (Lively et al., 2023).
